cases.abstract: Imitation policies trained on a few expert trajectories can fail when their own errors move the robot beyond demonstrated states. DMD addresses this mismatch by using a pose-conditioned diffusion model to synthesize wrist-camera views away from demonstration trajectories and pairing them with corrective action labels. The view model is adapted from pretrained weights using task demonstrations, task-agnostic play, or both; the policy learns from real and generated examples. Labels aim toward a later expert pose rather than the next frame, avoiding backward corrections when a sampled perturbation overshoots that frame. Real-robot experiments cover pushing, stacking, pouring, and shirt hanging. In ten apple-pushing trials per method with 24 demonstrations, DMD succeeds in all trials, versus 30% for behavior cloning and 50% for a replicated NeRF-based augmentation method. With eight demonstrations and a view model trained on play data, success is 80%, versus 20% for behavior cloning. With 1,447 cup-arrangement demonstrations, augmentation raises a diffusion policy's success from 4/25 to 16/25 for unseen cups in an unseen environment, with both methods using cropped, rectified images. These gains concern recoverable deviations: synthesized corrective supervision cannot undo irreversible events such as spilled contents.
cases.methods: DMD creates supervised recovery examples by perturbing the camera pose associated with an expert image, rather than merely changing that image's appearance. A pretrained latent diffusion model is fine-tuned on image pairs and their relative camera transforms, recovered from task or play trajectories using visual reconstruction. At generation time, a sampled local pose displacement conditions synthesis of a new wrist-camera view. Its action label is obtained by composing transforms from the virtual camera pose to a future expert pose. Choosing the immediately following frame can be counterproductive: a generated view may already lie beyond it, making the label direct the robot backward. Pushing experiments therefore use the third future frame, where offline angular error approximately plateaus. Training on the combined real and synthetic dataset exposes the policy to departures from expert trajectories while retaining supervision directed toward task progress.
cases.results: On apple pushing, adding diffusion-generated samples to color jitter and flips lowers median angular error from 0.355 to 0.328 radians, while online success with 24 demonstrations increases from 30% for behavior cloning to 100% for DMD over ten trials per method. The contrast is consistent with small prediction improvements limiting accumulated trajectory errors; the offline score alone does not establish that explanation. Play trajectories help view synthesis without being essential: task-only DMD achieves 80% pushing success, versus 100% with task and play data. Pouring also favors DMD under either training choice, but its 80% and 70% success rates come from separate randomized comparisons with different behavior-cloning baselines, 0% and 30%, potentially reflecting changed lighting or other conditions. These pouring figures cannot isolate the effect of play data. Overall, the results support augmentation for recoverable departures from demonstrations, not correction of irreversible failures such as spilling coffee beans.
cases.notes: The draft emphasizes corrective labeling rather than image generation alone. Eight-demonstration pushing still uses play data for view-model training. The 1,447-demonstration cup test uses retrained policies on cropped, rectified images, not the original fisheye configuration. Pouring comparisons retain their separate A/B conditions.

cases.abstract: Fine bimanual manipulation needs both affordable, responsive demonstration collection and policies that tolerate errors across long action sequences. ALOHA and Action Chunking with Transformers (ACT) address these requirements together. ALOHA is an open-source teleoperation system built within a USD 20,000 budget, using joint-space leader-follower control at 50 Hz and customized parallel-jaw grippers. ACT learns sequences of target joint positions from camera images and joint observations, reducing the effective prediction horizon while combining overlapping predictions to retain feedback and smooth motion. A conditional variational training objective accommodates variable human demonstrations. Evaluation covers two simulated tasks and six physical tasks; most physical policies use 50 demonstrations, while velcro threading uses 100. In 25 physical evaluations per method with one training seed, ACT achieves 88% success opening a slider bag and 96% inserting a battery, whereas four tuned baselines fail to complete either task. Ablations distinguish the benefits of chunking and generative training, and a six-person study finds faster teleoperation at 50 Hz than at 5 Hz. Performance remains uneven: velcro threading succeeds in only 20% of trials, and initial candy-unwrapping evaluation records no completed attempts in ten trials.
cases.methods: On ALOHA, Action Chunking with Transformers (ACT) predicts a chunk of future leader-arm joint targets from the follower arms' current joint positions and four camera views. Leader targets, rather than measured follower positions, preserve the command offsets through which the motor controllers exert force. Predicting several actions together shortens the effective decision horizon and can represent pauses or other temporally correlated behavior within a chunk. During deployment, the policy is queried at every control step, so chunks overlap. An exponentially weighted average combines predictions for the same execution time, smoothing transitions without averaging actions intended for different times. The transformer policy is trained as a conditional variational autoencoder: an encoder infers a latent style variable from demonstrated action sequences and joint observations, and the decoder reconstructs the sequence under a Gaussian-prior regularizer. At test time, the encoder is removed and the latent variable is fixed to zero, yielding deterministic action predictions.
cases.results: With temporal ensembling disabled, ACT's average success across two simulated tasks with scripted or human demonstrations rises from 1% for single-step prediction to 44% with 100-step chunks. Larger chunks slightly reduce performance, consistent with the cost of losing feedback and modeling longer sequences. Chunking also improves BC-ConvMLP and VINN, indicating that the gain is not exclusive to the transformer architecture. Removing conditional variational training barely changes performance on scripted demonstrations but reduces the human-data average from 35.3% to 2%; this comparison ties its benefit to variability in demonstrations rather than sequence prediction alone. Temporal ensembling is less uniformly helpful: separately tuned configurations improve ACT by 3.3 percentage points but reduce VINN from 37% to 17%. Physical task completion remains sensitive to perception, with velcro-threading success falling from 92% at lifting to 20% after insertion despite 100 demonstrations. Candy unwrapping yields 0/10 completed attempts initially; a later evaluation completes 3/5 candies but allows ten attempts per candy, so it measures a different retry budget.
cases.notes: The draft preserves ALOHA and ACT as co-contributions. Four-baseline comparisons apply to the two detailed physical tasks; the other four compare only with BeT. Temporal-ensemble configurations were tuned separately. The implementation text specifies L1 reconstruction, whereas the training pseudocode writes MSE, so the methods paragraph leaves the reconstruction metric unspecified. Candy results are separated by retry budget.
